incidents.title: Port scan from 192.168.1.66
incidents.summary: 192.168.1.66 probed 120 different ports on 192.168.1.30 with 120 connection attempts in 2.4 s. No open services were found.
incidents.cause: Someone running a scanning tool (e.g. a port scanner) from that machine, or malware on it looking for other devices to infect. It could also be an authorised security test.
steps: Identify who uses 192.168.1.66 and whether a security test was authorised.
If not authorised, isolate the machine and check it for malware.
Close or firewall any open services that don't need to be reachable.
for_attack: 192.168.1.66 tried 120 different ports on 192.168.1.30 in 2.4 s, checking which services are open.
Very fast: about 50 connection attempts per second, faster than any person could click.
Almost none of these attempts were used to exchange data. The goal was only to see which ports answered.

incidents.title: DNS server 192.168.1.1 is not answering
incidents.summary: 15 of 15 name lookups sent to 192.168.1.1 got no answer (e.g. api.example.net, cdn.example.net, docs.example.org and 4 more).
incidents.cause: The DNS server (often the router) is down, overloaded or unreachable, or devices were given the wrong DNS server address.
steps: Try another resolver to confirm: nslookup example.com 1.1.1.1 vs nslookup example.com 192.168.1.1
Restart the DNS service on 192.168.1.1 (or the router if it's the router).
Check the DNS server address handed out by DHCP.
for_fault: 15 of 15 lookups sent to 192.168.1.1 never got an answer.

incidents.title: Two devices are using the same IP address (192.168.1.50)
incidents.summary: The address 192.168.1.50 is being used by 2 different devices: 02:00:00:00:01:32 and 0a:1b:2c:3d:4e:50. Each one behaves like a normal computer, so this looks like a configuration mistake, not an attack.
incidents.cause: A device with a manually set (static) IP that is also inside the DHCP pool, or two devices configured with the same static address.
steps: Find both devices by their MAC addresses (router's client list / switch MAC table).
Give one of them a different address, or switch it to DHCP.
Reserve static addresses outside the DHCP range.
for_fault: Each device claims only this one address, which looks like two machines that were given the same IP by mistake.
The devices only announced themselves or answered real questions. Nobody pushed unsolicited replies.

incidents.title: ARP spoofing: de:ad:be:ef:00:66 is impersonating 192.168.1.1
incidents.summary: The device with hardware address de:ad:be:ef:00:66 is telling the network that it is 192.168.1.1 (your gateway/router) and also as 192.168.1.20. The real owner of 192.168.1.1 is 00:11:22:33:44:01. This is a man-in-the-middle setup: traffic meant for 192.168.1.1 is being redirected through the attacker.
incidents.cause: Someone on the local network is running an ARP spoofing tool (e.g. a man-in-the-middle toolkit), or a device there is infected with malware.
steps: Find the switch port of MAC de:ad:be:ef:00:66 (switch MAC table) and disconnect it.
Enable Dynamic ARP Inspection / DHCP snooping on managed switches.
Set a static ARP entry for 192.168.1.1 on critical machines as a stop-gap.
for_attack: de:ad:be:ef:00:66 is also claiming to be 192.168.1.20. A normal network card has one address; one device pretending to be several is the signature of ARP spoofing.
de:ad:be:ef:00:66 sent 15 ARP replies nobody asked for, trying to overwrite other devices' memory of who 192.168.1.1 is.
The fake replies repeat like clockwork (every ~2.0 s), the way a poisoning tool refreshes the lie before it expires.
The address being taken over (192.168.1.1) is the network gateway. Whoever owns it can see all internet traffic.
de:ad:be:ef:00:66 is also claiming to be 192.168.1.1. A normal network card has one address; one device pretending to be several is the signature of ARP spoofing.
de:ad:be:ef:00:66 sent 15 ARP replies nobody asked for, trying to overwrite other devices' memory of who 192.168.1.20 is.

catalog.title: Healthy office network
catalog.description: 40 seconds of normal office traffic: web browsing, DNS lookups and ARP. Includes realistic noise that must NOT raise alarms: one lost packet in a long download and one mistyped domain name.

catalog.title: Slow website - lossy link
catalog.description: Three office PCs download from the same web server over a congested link. About 1 in 8 packets is lost and re-sent, which makes pages crawl even though the network looks 'up'.

catalog.title: DNS server is down
catalog.description: The router's DNS service stopped answering. Users retry lookups and nothing resolves, yet connections made directly to IP addresses still work, which proves the link itself is fine.

catalog.title: Two PCs with the same IP
catalog.description: A second machine boots with a static IP (192.168.1.50) that another PC already uses. Both answer ARP for it, so connections randomly break. Classic misconfiguration, not an attack.

catalog.title: MTU black hole over VPN
catalog.description: A VPN link only fits 1400-byte packets. Small requests work, but large data packets vanish and are re-sent forever, the 'page half-loads' problem. A router reports 'packet too big' once.

catalog.title: Port scan from inside the LAN
catalog.description: Device 192.168.1.66 probes 250 ports on a server in a couple of seconds, finding SSH, HTTP and HTTPS open. This is reconnaissance, the step before an attack.

catalog.title: ARP spoofing (man-in-the-middle)
catalog.description: An attacker keeps telling the victim 'I am the router' and the router 'I am the victim' every 2 seconds, so all of the victim's traffic flows through the attacker's machine.

catalog.title: DNS hijacking
catalog.description: When the victim looks up a bank and a shop, a machine on the LAN races a forged answer pointing to itself, arriving before the real DNS server's reply.

catalog.title: Rogue DHCP server
catalog.description: An unauthorised DHCP server answers new devices faster than the real one and hands out ITSELF as router and DNS server, a stealthy way to intercept every new device.

catalog.title: Crashed service + slow server
catalog.description: Four PCs keep getting 'connection refused' from an internal app on port 8080 (the service is down), while a remote server answers every request after ~650 ms.
catalog.expected: FAULT: service refusing connections + FAULT: high latency

catalog.title: Outage AND attack at once (pcapng)
catalog.description: The hardest case: DNS is down (a fault) while, at the same time, someone scans a server (an attack). Both look like 'the network is broken'; PacketMedic separates them.
catalog.expected: FAULT: DNS failure + ATTACK: port scan

catalog.title: Extra DHCP server (misconfig)
catalog.description: Someone plugged a home router into the office network. It hands out addresses too, but with the SAME router/DNS settings, so it is a mistake, not an attack. Tests the fault-vs-attack judgement.

catalog.title: Hostile DNS names (injection test)
catalog.description: DNS lookups for names containing <script> tags, HTML and terminal markup. Proves that untrusted packet data is displayed safely everywhere and never executed.

catalog.title: Corrupted / malicious file
catalog.description: Valid packets, then random garbage, then a record that claims to be 4 GB long. The tool must not crash or run out of memory; it reports what it could read plus warnings.

catalog.title: Fake .pcap (text file)
catalog.description: A plain text file renamed to .pcap. It must be rejected up front with a clear message.
